jTVpg%5ap0xD3|DkEx/*.text: 1 Line Challenge------------------------The 1 Line Challenge is to produce an interesting pattern on the screen using only one  line of code to calculate the color of each pixel.This program moves to all points in a big square on the screen and draws a dot at each with the color determined by the "set pen color to ..." block.This is the Only Line you can change to meet the 1 Line Challenge!------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------AND you must change it to another "set pen color to ..." statement.You may also change the project name to reflect the pattern produced and add comments to explain your single line of code.Please credit and quote any known fancy formulae you use but preferably use your own ideas.You will most likely use the xposition and yposition of a pixel in your calculation to set a pixel's color.Studio for your "1 Line Challenge" Projects----------------------------------------------------------Put your completed projects (remixes) in the studio "1 Line Challenge" at https://scratch.mit.edu/studios/2825709/Please give your projects a thumbnail picture.  (Run your project to produce the pattern, move any block of code slightly, and use File, Save Now).If you just had to break the rules please put your projects in the studio "Not Quite a 1 Line Project" instead https://scratch.mit.edu/studios/2825759/Rewards:    This is not a contest.  I will not be judging a winner.-------------     ---------------------------   ---------------------------------------Your rewards come from other Scratchers seeing your projects in the studio and loving, favoriting or commenting nicely on them.** More Rules after the code below **             A Short Tutorial in the Tutorial Sprite---------------------------------------------------             -------------------------------------------------**  A Big Tutorial Added for Scratch Programmers  **  Read the Short Tutorial First!  **

+}1}^RsH35m#xgmhKg46.text: More Rules---------------- - The project must have at least 2 colors. (sorry to the real zen programmers).- You may use either version of the "set pen color to ..." block.I recommend the "set pen color to number" version which uses the Scratch colors from 0 to 200.  (Numbers outside this range still convert to Scratch colors and just cycle around the 200 colours again).- No custom blocks or hacked blocks (functions do not exist in Scratch 2.0).- You cannot add lines of code.(This rule is for pedantic programmers who might note that the rules previously said you could only change one line but said nothing about adding lines).- No new variables, lists, sprites or costumes to be added to the project!  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------(Thank-you conwayslife for alerting me to this).- No extra Title Screens or Animations (unless they are in the 1 Line you can change).   ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ No more completely random color projects - we have one.But using random is ok - lots of patterns that have static or blur use the random operator.Yet More Rules with Things you Can Do!-------------------------------------------------------- You may change the row length to 480 so that your pattern covers the whole screen.- You may shift the "Pen Down" before the "Repeat 360" loop and the "Pen Up" after it.   (This improves the speed of the code slightly) - You may also delete the two purple Comment blocks in the loop for the same reason.The managers and curators may occaisionally admit projects to the "1 Line Challenge" studio which break some rules, but there is a special reason to admit them.

Bz7{A@8{onZK,QbGBOt0.text: 200 Rainbow Colors  (using the first block above)----------------------------If you want to use the continuous range of Scratch colours from 0 to 200 you will sometimes need to multiply the result of your color calculation by 200 to get this color range.6 Colors (or 4 Colors)------------------------------If you only want to use 6 colors in your pattern, do the following:set pen color to  33 * ( floor of  ( 6 * ( your fancy formula mod 1)  )  )"your fancy formula" mod 1  gives you a number between 0 and 1Multiply it by 6 to get a number between 0 and 6"Floor of "  converts this number to 0,1,2,3,4 or 5Multiply by 33 gives you 6 well spaced distinct colors in the range 0 to 200.NB. If you use this formula you need numbers with a decimal part so use division or the sqrt, sin, cos operators etc at the bottom of the central light green operators tab.NB. Multiply by 4 and 50 rather than 6 and 33 for 4 colors.        More than about 8 colors is difficult as the Scratch colors are similar.

yYKAI`Kw];?mHtX@o{J..text: 1) Your Screen is Half Red  (or 1/4 red or 3/4 red)     ---------------------------------     (And How To Make Symmetrical Designs)      -------------------------------------------------------The usual reason that the left half of your screen is red is that you have used eithersqrt (xposition)  or log(xposition) or ln(xposition)    or 10^(xposition) or e^(xposition).These are all invalid mathematical expressions when xposition is negative.Scratch replaces the result by zero - which is the Scratch color red.How to fix it!Use sqrt (abs (xposition)), log(abs (xposition)) or ln(abs (xposition))  etcThe abs operator converts all numbers to positive numbers.You will get nice symmetrical designs when you use abs (xposition) everywhere or abs(yposition) everywhere or both!2) The Top Right Corner of Your Screen is Black     --------------------------------------------------------------     (And how to add BLACK to your Scratch Colours) - after the demo!       ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------When numbers get really really really big, Scratch cannot handle them anymore.  Scratch sets the color to black.Usually you have    10 ^ (xposition + yposition)When xposition + yposition get to about 310 that is a 1 with 310 zeroes after it.That is quite a big number.  The top right hand corner of the screen goes black with xposition + yposition being bigger than 310.CLICK THE CODE BLOCK BELOW - It looks great and demonstarates both red and black areas.

(This is the left half of the screen).When xposition is positive, Your #2 Formula  is combined with  Your #2 Formula.

1K,Xv%3i#Ubba~Qe7h@].text: RGB COLOUR--------------------rgb means Red Green Blue.We can represent a colour as a combination of three primary colour components:red 0-255, green 0-255 and blue 0-255(0 means none of a colour, 255 means full strength of a colour)                                                                  red  green   blueeg.  Full Red      is represented as    255,         0,        0       Full Green   is represented as         0,    255,        0       Full Blue      is represented as         0,         0,   255       Black            is represented as         0,        0,        0       White            is represented as    255,    255,    255The red, green and blue colour components each have 256 possible values from 0 to 255.There are 256 x 256 x 256 = 16,777,216 different colours that each pixel can be represented by using this rgb colour model. (This is 24 bit colour - see below).The program does all the conversions from r,g,b colour components to one rgb colour number and vice versa.To convert the three red, green, blue components to one number:       Colour = red * 65536 + green * 256 + blue(256 * 256 = 65536)

}^1w36DcLqz.*UudU{hs.text: RGB Colors in a Different Format---------------------------------------------If you look up RGB Colors on the Internet, the color numbers you see will not normally be decimal numbers like in the box above.They will either be expressed in red, green, blue components:                      red    green     blue   Yellow       255     255           0   Magenta    255          0       255   Cyan               0     255        255or they will be expressed in Hexadecimal (base 16) numbers    Yellow       FFFF00    Magenta    FF00FF    Cyan          00FFFF    Red            FF0000    Green        00FF00    Blue           0000FF    Black          000000    White          FFFFFFYou can use these Hexadecimal numbers for RGB Colors even if you don't quite understand how they work!!!Look up "RGB Colors" on the Internet for the codes for any color you want.We put Hexadecimal numbers into Scratch using the "join" operator as below - the 0x at the front kind of means hexadecimal (I don't want to confuse you) and the color yellow is FFFF00.

a)jv6)B}i2WLVk[+bBK*.text: A Final Note about RGB Color: How it works in Binary (Base 2)-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Yes computers do really work on 0s and 1s!Each R, G, B component is really stored as a binary number from 00000000 to 11111111.We can store each component colour in 8 bits or 1 byte.The three colour components can be stored together like this giving us 24 bit colour.                                                                                                                                 -----------------eg. Pure Red     in binary is 11111111 00000000 00000000 (without the spaces)       Pure Green in binary is 00000000 11111111 00000000       Pure Blue    in binary is 00000000 00000000 11111111The combined RGB Colour number consists of 3 bytes:  8 bits for a red value from 0 to 255, then  8 bits for a green value from 0 to 255, then  8 bits for a blue value from 0 to 255.
